title: How to Actually Forgive Your Spouse
excerpt: Forgiveness is not pretending it did not happen, and it is not a feeling that arrives on its own. It is a decision, often made before the feeling catches up.
body:
Two sinners cannot share a life without wounding each other, daily, in ways large and small, and a marriage is finally only as durable as its capacity to forgive. We know this in theory. In practice we are terrible at it, partly because no one ever taught us what forgiveness actually is, and so we confuse it with several things it is not and then resent it for failing to do what it was never meant to do.

Let me clear the ground first, because most of the trouble with forgiveness comes from misunderstanding it.

## What forgiveness is not

Forgiveness is not saying it did not matter. The opposite. You only forgive what was real, what cost you something. Minimizing the wound is not forgiveness, it is denial, and denial does not heal, it buries, and buried things do not stay buried.

Forgiveness is not the same as trust. You can forgive a spouse who lied to you and still require that trust be rebuilt over time through changed behavior. Forgiveness is given freely. Trust is earned back slowly. Confusing the two is how people get told to immediately trust someone who has given them no reason to, which is not grace, it is foolishness.

Forgiveness is not always reconciliation. Forgiveness takes one person. Reconciliation takes two, and requires the offender to own what they did. You can forgive someone who refuses to repent, but you cannot have full reconciliation with them, and you should not pretend you do.

And forgiveness is not a feeling. This is the one that traps people. They wait to feel forgiving, and the feeling does not come, and they conclude they have not forgiven and never will. Forgiveness is first a decision, a releasing of the debt, made by the will, often while the feelings are still raw. The feelings follow later, sometimes much later, sometimes in waves with relapses in between.

## What forgiveness is

Forgiveness is releasing the right to make them pay. That is the core of it. When someone wrongs you, they incur a debt, and you have a right to collect, by punishing, by withholding, by bringing it up, by keeping the wound on the books so you can charge interest on it for years. To forgive is to cancel the debt, to give up the right to collect, to absorb the cost yourself rather than extract it from them.

This is exactly what the cross is. Paul says, forgive one another as God in Christ forgave you. Not as they deserve. As you were forgiven, which is to say at someone else's cost, freely, before you had earned it. The reason a Christian can forgive a real wrong is not that the wrong was small but that their own enormous debt has already been cleared, and a person who has been forgiven much loses the standing to hold a small account against someone else. The unforgiving servant in Jesus' parable is not condemned for being wronged. He is condemned for choking a fellow servant over a few coins while standing forgiven of a fortune.

## How to actually do it

Name the wound specifically. Vague forgiveness does not work because vague wounds do not heal. Say to yourself, and if it is safe to the marriage, to your spouse, exactly what was done and exactly how it hurt. You said you would be there and you were not, and I felt alone and humiliated. You cannot release a debt you have not named.

Decide to release it. This is a definite act, often a spoken one, even if only to God. I release my right to make you pay for this. I will not bring it up as a weapon. I will not collect on it. This is the hinge. Everything before it is preparation and everything after it is follow-through, but this is where the forgiveness actually happens, in the will, before the feelings have moved.

Then keep deciding it. Forgiveness for a deep wound is not one decision but a hundred, because the wound will resurface, the memory will rise with the old fire on it, and the resentment will ask for the right back. Each time, you release it again. This is not failure. This is what forgiving a serious wrong looks like from the inside, a daily handing back of a debt you keep instinctively picking up. Over time the grip loosens. The feelings catch up. The wound becomes a scar instead of an open thing.

## When the wound is severe

For betrayal, for the deep wounds, forgiveness does not mean you skip the process of grieving and rebuilding. It does not mean you cannot require honesty, accountability, sometimes outside help. Forgiveness and consequences can coexist. You can forgive and still say, I forgive you, and we are going to counseling, and you are going to rebuild my trust, because the forgiveness is about my heart and the rebuilding is about our marriage, and both have to happen.

And a word of caution: forgiveness is not a tool for keeping someone trapped in danger. If you are being abused, forgiving in your heart is one thing, and it does not require you to stay in harm's way or to pretend the danger is not real. Get safe first. Forgiveness was never meant to be a chain.

## This week

Take the one resentment you keep picking back up, the wound you have rehearsed a hundred times. Name it specifically, on paper or out loud to God, exactly what was done and how it hurt. Then make the actual decision: I release my right to make them pay for this. You will have to make it again tomorrow, and the day after. Make it anyway. The couples who last are not the ones who stopped wounding each other. They are the ones who never stopped forgiving, who kept the account short because they remembered how long their own account with God had been, and how completely it was cleared.
